opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fun question, because when AlphaGo came out in 2016, DeepMind needed an enormous amount of compute, and a lot of the cleverness in that system was really about squeezing performance out of a constrained budget. Now you can rent a few modern GPUs and get surprisingly far, and that changes which ideas actually matter.

The biggest shift is that a lot of the hand-engineering just becomes unnecessary. The original AlphaGo had the supervised policy network trained on human games, a separate rollout policy, a value network, and fast rollouts mixed into the evaluation. With faster hardware you realize much of that scaffolding was compensating for not being able to run the neural network enough times. Once inference is cheap, you lean almost entirely on the network: a good value head, a good policy head, and Monte Carlo tree search on top. That's basically the AlphaZero recipe, and it's strikingly simple.

What still matters a lot, maybe more than people expect, is the engineering of the self-play loop. How fast can you generate games? How do you batch network evaluations across many parallel searches so the GPU is always saturated? Are your data pipeline and replay buffer bottlenecking training? With fast GPUs, the hardware usually isn't the limiting factor anymore. The software around it is. Things like KataGo's improvements, auxiliary prediction targets like ownership and score, and randomizing playout counts so you get more useful training signal per game, give you big multiples in efficiency, and those compound.

The other thing I'd highlight is that faster compute makes it easier to iterate. You can run an experiment in a day instead of a month, which means you can actually check whether a trick helps instead of copying it on faith. When I tried rebuilding these systems, a lot of the folklore didn't hold up at smaller scales, and some unglamorous details, like how you handle the value target or the temperature schedule early in games, mattered far more than the architectural choices people argue about.

So the summary is that faster GPUs have shifted the emphasis from clever algorithmic workarounds to throughput, data efficiency, and quick iteration. The core idea, search plus a learned evaluator improving itself, has stayed the same. Everything else is about how efficiently you can turn compute into good training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that's interesting about Go specifically is that it's kind of a laboratory for this question, because we have this really clean before-and-after. AlphaGo in 2016 was this enormous engineering effort, and then AlphaGo Zero and then the open-source reproductions like Leela Zero and KataGo came after. And what you see is that a lot of the cleverness in the original system was really compensating for a compute budget that no longer binds in the same way.

So when I think about what faster GPUs changed, the first thing is that they changed what counts as a "trick" versus what counts as a crutch. The original AlphaGo had a separate rollout policy, this fast linear thing that ran on CPU, supervised learning on human games to bootstrap, a value net trained on a carefully de-correlated dataset. Each of those was a reasonable engineering decision given the hardware. And then as soon as you have enough throughput to just do self-play at scale with a single network doing policy and value together, most of that stuff falls away. It wasn't that those ideas were wrong, it's that they were solving a problem that the hardware now solves for you.

The second thing, and I think this is underappreciated, is that the bottleneck moved. Once the network evaluation is cheap, the question becomes: how many games can you generate per hour, and how much signal do you extract from each one? So the techniques that matter now are much more about data efficiency on the self-play side. KataGo is the clearest example of this. David Wu got something like a fifty-x reduction in compute versus Leela Zero, and almost none of that came from a better architecture. It came from things like auxiliary targets, predicting ownership of every point on the board, predicting score, not just win/loss. Playout cap randomization, where you spend a lot of search on a few moves and very little on most of them so you don't waste GPU time generating training targets for positions that don't need it. Global pooling so the network can actually see things like ko threats and komi. Those are all "how do I get more gradient per GPU-second" ideas, and they only become the thing you optimize once the raw evaluation cost stopped being the thing you were fighting.

The third thing I'd say is that fast hardware makes search itself more valuable, not less, which is a little counterintuitive. People sometimes assume the trajectory is: more compute, bigger net, eventually you don't need MCTS. And that's not really what happened. What happened is that MCTS got cheaper, so you can afford more playouts per training example, and the policy improvement operator gets stronger, and the whole loop converges faster. So the lesson I take from that is that if you have a good way to spend inference compute to get a better target than the network alone would produce, faster hardware amplifies that rather than obsoleting it. That generalizes well beyond Go, I think.

And then maybe the last point, which is more of a cultural one. When compute was scarce, there was a lot of value in having really deep domain knowledge about Go, handcrafted features, pattern libraries, all of that. The hardware getting faster shifted the value toward people who understand the training dynamics of the system as a whole. Like, why does the value net overfit? Why does the policy collapse on ladders? Those are machine learning questions, not Go questions. So if you were rebuilding a strong Go engine today, I'd honestly tell you to spend very little time on architecture, moderate time on search, and most of your time on the self-play data pipeline and what you're asking the network to predict. The GPUs are good enough that the clever part is almost entirely in how you generate and use the data.

astra-6.text:
I think faster GPUs change what’s worth spending engineering effort on. With Go, you can put a lot of sophistication into the search—how you explore the tree, how you evaluate positions, all these little optimizations. But as neural network inference gets cheaper, you can afford a stronger policy and value network, and that can make some of those clever tricks less important.

The interesting thing is that you wouldn’t necessarily rebuild a strong Go system today by faithfully reproducing every detail of an older one. You’d want to ask: which details were fundamental, and which were ways of coping with the hardware budget at the time? Search still matters, but the balance between spending compute on search and spending it on a better network can shift. Faster hardware changes the algorithm you should choose, not just how quickly the old algorithm runs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’ve changed what’s worth being clever about. If you were rebuilding a strong Go AI today, I wouldn’t assume you need to reproduce every component of the original AlphaGo. You’d want to ask which components were compensating for the compute constraints at the time.

Take the rollout policy. In the original system, you had this fast policy that could play a game out to the end and give you an estimate of who would win. That was useful because evaluating everything with a big neural network was expensive. As neural network inference gets faster, you can spend more of your budget on a stronger policy and value network, and the case for maintaining that separate rollout machinery becomes weaker.

But hardware doesn’t make every algorithmic idea irrelevant. Search still lets you spend additional computation on the particular position in front of you. The interesting question is how to allocate your compute between training a better network and searching more at inference time. Faster GPUs move that balance, so the best recipe isn’t necessarily the historical recipe run faster.
